references.text: Jesus posed the counter-question of whether John's baptism was from heaven or from humans ([ref:Luk 20:3-4|Luke 20:3-4]). Verse 5 records their internal reasoning about the consequences of answering "from heaven," which would mean they should have believed John.

The people and tax collectors gave God right when they were baptized with John's baptism, but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected God's plan for them ([ref:Luk 7:29-30|Luke 7:29-30]). This is the background for why the religious leaders knew that Jesus would expose their unbelief toward John.

The parallel text in [ref:Matt 21:25|Matthew 21:25] presents the same reasoning, where they discuss among themselves and realize that the answer "from heaven" would reveal that they did not believe John.
The parallel text in [ref:Mark 11:31|Mark 11:31] describes the same internal discussion among the religious leaders, with identical argumentation that Jesus would ask why they did not believe John.
Jesus later pointed out that John came to them in the way of righteousness, but they did not believe him ([ref:Matt 21:32|Matthew 21:32]), confirming that their unbelief toward John was well known.

Jesus testified that John was a lamp that burned and shone, and that he bore witness to the truth ([ref:Joh 5:33-35|John 5:33-35]). The religious leaders' lack of faith in John was thus also a rejection of the true testimony.
When the Jewish leaders sent priests and Levites to John to ask who he was, they received clear information about his mission ([ref:Joh 1:19-27|John 1:19-27]), but still chose not to believe in him.
